items.title: Grow the aluminium contacts in the chamber and ZnSe conducts at 5 K
items.dek: A Forschungszentrum Jülich and RWTH Aachen group built working field-effect transistors in zinc selenide — a wide-bandgap compound semiconductor whose contacts normally stop conducting when cooled — by depositing the aluminium source and drain inside the growth chamber, and measured gate control down to 5 kelvin.
items.why_it_matters: Every ohmic contact to n-type zinc selenide has previously needed a post-growth anneal, and the anneal is what breaks it: metal diffusing into the crystal leaves group-II vacancies that act as acceptors and compensate the donors, so the contact goes high-resistance exactly when you cool it. Depositing the metal without an anneal removes that mechanism instead of working around it. The measured subthreshold swing then says where the remaining loss sits — 73 millivolts per decade at 5 kelvin, where the thermodynamic floor kT/q·ln10 is about 1 — so the oxide interface, not the channel, is now what limits the device.
items.background_md: Zinc selenide is a II–VI compound semiconductor wide enough in bandgap to emit blue light, and the reason anyone wants it for electronics is isotopic: zinc, selenium and sulphur all have abundant isotopes with zero nuclear spin, so a purified crystal is a magnetically quiet host for a single electron spin. The obstacle has always been contacts. Making a metal conduct into n-type ZnSe normally requires annealing it into the surface, and the anneal damages the crystal; a contact that is merely resistive at room temperature can freeze out entirely once carriers lose thermal energy.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is grown by molecular-beam epitaxy on GaAs: a 300 nm GaAs buffer, a 10 nm ZnSe seed layer, ZnMgSe barriers, a 50 nm heavily n-doped ZnSe contact layer, then 20 nm Al₂O₃ and 5 nm HfO₂ as gate dielectric under a Ti/Au gate. The trick is a silicon shadow wall about 1.95 µm tall standing on the wafer and blocking the incoming flux, so the doped regions and the 60 nm aluminium source/drain are both patterned by line of sight during growth and the metal never leaves vacuum. Zn and Se adatoms diffuse very little, which is why a shadow produces an abrupt edge rather than a graded one.

Measured: field-effect mobility 101 cm²/V·s at 300 K, rising to 116 at 5 K; threshold near 3.5 V; on/off above 10⁷; drain current from below 1 pA off to about 80 µA at 6 V gate. Subthreshold swing falls from 145 to 73 mV/dec on cooling — a factor of two, over a range where the thermal limit falls by about sixty.

The authors name the gap themselves: traps at the ZnSe/oxide interface, with a simulated intrinsic low-field mobility near 200 cm²/V·s, roughly double what they measure. No spin has been confined in these devices. This is a transistor; the qubit is a plan, and the same group's single-spin work so far is optical rather than electrical.

glossary.definition: A metal–semiconductor junction whose current is proportional to voltage in both directions rather than rectifying; getting one needs the metal's work function to line up with the band edge, or the barrier to be thin enough to tunnel through.

The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold below threshold; kT/q·ln10 sets the floor — about 60 mV/decade at 300 K, about 1 at 5 K — so a swing that ignores temperature means trapped charge.

Growing and metallising through a tall physical wall standing on the wafer, so layers and contacts are patterned by line of sight during growth instead of by resist afterwards, and the metal interface never meets air.
Crystal growth from elemental beams evaporated in ultra-high vacuum onto a heated substrate, slowly enough that composition and thickness are controlled to a fraction of a monolayer.

items.fab_angle: The in-situ metallisation is the part worth stealing: it says a source/drain contact can be defined with no lithography at all, by a wall tall enough to cast a shadow across the deposition flux. The trade is alignment accuracy for interface quality, and it only works for materials whose adatoms barely diffuse once they land.

items.title: Tin in GST halves the energy it takes to crystallise a photonic switch
items.dek: Nathan Youngblood's group at Pittsburgh, with Queen's University and Maryland, alloyed tin into Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ — the chalcogenide that stores a bit by flipping between glassy and crystalline — and cut the heater energy needed to crystallise a silicon waveguide switch from 3.22 to 1.46 microjoules.
items.why_it_matters: Phase-change photonic switches have so far been made cheaper to program by redesigning the heater and the waveguide around the material; this changes the material and leaves the device untouched, so the gain composes with every geometric trick already applied rather than competing with it. The mechanism is bond energy: substituting tin for germanium replaces Ge–Te bonds of at least 396 kJ/mol with Sn–Te bonds near 360, lowering the cohesive energy of the network and with it the barrier to reordering. The same substitution sets its own ceiling, because it darkens the amorphous state, so the useful range closes at both ends.
items.background_md: A chalcogenide like Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ has two solid states with very different optical constants: an amorphous one, reached by melting the material and quenching it faster than it can order, and a crystalline one, reached by holding it above the glass transition long enough to let it order. Both are stable at room temperature, so a switch built from one holds its state on no power at all. The cost is paid at write time, because the amorphising pulse has to genuinely melt the patch — which is why programming energy, not static power, limits how many such switches a photonic circuit can carry.
items.deeper_md:
The devices are silicon-on-insulator Mach–Zehnder interferometers with a 2 µm-wide phase-change patch on one arm, driven by a doped PN or PIN microheater in the slab and capped with 60 nm of ALD Al₂O₃ against oxidation. Tin was co-sputtered at 0, 5, 10 and 20 at.%.

On the PN heater, amorphisation energy falls from about 303 nJ undoped to 216 nJ at 5 at.% and 185 nJ at 10, then rises again to 198 at 20. Crystallisation falls from 3.22 µJ to 1.46 µJ at 10 at.%. PIN heaters show the same shape at lower absolute energies, up to roughly 4× on crystallisation and 1.5× on amorphisation.

The reversal at 20 at.% is the informative failure: TEM composition analysis points to crystalline SnTe segregating out, so the alloy stops being an alloy. A second ceiling arrives earlier — absorption modulation contrast falls monotonically from 9.0 undoped to 0.3 at 20 at.% as the amorphous state itself becomes absorbing, which is what makes 10 at.% the practical limit for C-band amplitude work.

Endurance is the open question the authors name. A 10 at.% device survived 1,000 cycles, but extinction ratio decayed from 4.5 ± 0.3 dB to 2.4 ± 0.3 dB, and post-cycling imaging shows material migrating toward the patch edge and leaving voids. They argue that is an encapsulation problem rather than a chemistry one; nobody has shown that yet.

glossary.definition: The chalcogenide alloy behind rewritable optical discs and phase-change memory, chosen because it crystallises in nanoseconds yet stays amorphous indefinitely at room temperature.
Composition counted by number of atoms rather than by mass — the convention for alloys whose constituents have very different atomic weights, and the one that matters when you are counting bonds.
The optical power difference between a switch's two states, in decibels; it sets how many stages can be cascaded before the on and off levels start to overlap.
A resistive element — here the doped silicon slab beside the waveguide — used to deliver a shaped current pulse into the phase-change patch without putting lossy metal inside the optical mode.

items.fab_angle: The whole change lives in the sputter target. Co-sputtering a second element into an existing film and capping it with ALD alumina are both steps a university tool set can run, and the result says a materials knob was sitting unturned while the field optimised geometry. The failure mode is recognisable too: a patch that reflows and voids after a thousand thermal cycles is an encapsulation problem before it is a chemistry one.

items.title: Dicing glass with a beam that evaporates instead of exploding
items.dek: Razvan Stoian's group at Saint-Étienne, with collaborators at Northwestern Polytechnical University, cut 100-micrometre aluminosilicate glass in a single pass with a non-diffracting laser beam and left sidewalls rough to only 3 to 5 nanometres, about fifty times smoother than stress-induced laser dicing.
items.why_it_matters: The removal mechanism is the finding, not the roughness number. Conventional ultrafast dicing deposits enough energy to blow material out violently, and the fracture surface that leaves is the reason diced glass then needs grinding and polishing before anyone can use the edge. Confining the same pulse energy into a near-field spot drops the deposition into a regime where the surface simply evaporates, a few molecular layers at a time, from a region held at 3,000 to 4,000 kelvin. The finish is then set by thermodynamics rather than by where the cracks happened to run — and the post-processing step that exists to repair the cracks becomes optional.
items.background_md: A femtosecond pulse focused inside transparent glass is absorbed nonlinearly: the intensity is high enough to ionise material that was transparent a moment earlier, and the resulting plasma dumps its energy into a volume smaller than the focal spot. An ordinary lens gives a focus a few micrometres long, so cutting through a 100 µm sheet means many passes at many depths. A Bessel beam removes that limit — a conical wavefront whose central core stays in focus for hundreds of micrometres. What that core does to the glass then depends on how hard it is driven.
items.deeper_md:
The beam is a 0th-order Bessel–Gauss formed from 1.03 µm pulses of 200 fs (and 1.5 ps for comparison) at a nominal 100 kHz, with a 1.1 µm FWHM core and a 120 µm Bessel length in air — long enough to span the 0.1 mm Schott AS 87 eco samples in one pass, which separate cleanly in two with comparable damage on front and back faces.

Roughness comes out at Ra ≈ 4 nm for the femtosecond case and ≈ 5 nm for the picosecond one measured along the laser's passage, and ≈ 3 nm along the scan direction for both. The stated benchmark for laser stress-induced dicing is above 100 nm, hence the factor of fifty.

The mechanism claim rests on Hertz–Knudsen evaporation: at a sustained 3,000–4,000 K the paper computes evaporation timescales of several nanoseconds per monolayer, which is slow and orderly compared with explosive ejection. The near-field confinement is what makes that possible, and it decouples kerf from spot size — the transverse section is reported at 10 nm, more than 100× smaller than the beam waist and about a hundredth of the wavelength, narrowing toward 6 nm as the scan pitch is reduced to 1 nm.

Two things to hold against it. The picosecond pulses visibly corrugate the surface more than the femtosecond ones, so the regime is narrow. And the 1 nm pitch is reached at a 0.1 mm/s scan speed — one millimetre of cut every ten seconds, which makes this a mechanism result rather than a tool.

glossary.definition: A beam formed by conical interference whose central core does not spread with distance and reconstructs itself after an obstruction, giving a focus hundreds of micrometres long instead of a few.
The average absolute deviation of a surface from its mean line; a few nanometres is optical quality, while a crack-dominated fracture surface is typically hundreds.
Atom flux leaving a hot surface, set by the gap between its vapour pressure and the ambient partial pressure; it removes material a monolayer at a time rather than ejecting fragments.
The width of material a cutting process consumes. Narrower kerf means more usable die per panel and less mechanical stress driven into the cut edge.

items.fab_angle: A teaching cleanroom dices with a saw and lives with chipped edges, and the usual lesson is that edge quality is a property of the tool class. This says it is a property of the energy-deposition regime instead. The number to carry away is the pitch–width coupling: once removal is evaporative, the trench narrows as the scan pitch falls, so the beam width stops being what sets the feature size.

items.title: Flash wears out, so cache admission becomes a lifetime budget
items.dek: A Berkeley and FuriosaAI team simulated serving large language models out of High Bandwidth Flash — stacked NAND sitting beside the accelerator where high-bandwidth DRAM normally goes — and found that reserving a tenth of its capacity triples the flash's estimated write life, from 4.77 to 14.82 years.
items.why_it_matters: This brief covered the provisioning half of the argument on 15 September: move model weights into flash and the DRAM left behind needs 8 to 24 times less bandwidth per byte than HBM3e. What changes now is that someone has put a number on the bill. A flash cell tolerates a finite count of program/erase cycles, so every cached key-value entry written to the device spends part of a fixed lifetime, and the admission policy that decides what gets written is therefore also deciding how long the hardware lasts. Nothing in a DRAM-based hierarchy behaves that way, so no existing serving scheduler has a term for it.
items.background_md: A flash cell stores charge behind a tunnel barrier, and writing it means pushing carriers through that barrier hard enough to damage it slightly each time. The damage accumulates, so a cell carries a rating in program/erase cycles — tens of thousands for the dense multi-level kind — after which it no longer holds a level reliably. DRAM has no equivalent counter; it fails on entirely different terms. Any design that puts flash where DRAM used to sit therefore inherits a budget nobody previously had to schedule against: total bytes written across the part's service life.
items.deeper_md:
The modelled part is one HBF stack against one HBM stack: 375 GB versus 24 GB, both reading at 1,000 GB/s, but HBF writing at 8 GB/s behind a 250 µs startup against HBM's 1,000 GB/s and 0.1 µs. Energy is asymmetric the same way — 6.8 pJ/bit to read HBF against 3.4 for HBM, and 100 pJ/bit to write it. Endurance is assumed at 100,000 program/erase cycles.

The scheduling knob is a single number. Admission requires L + Aᵢ ≤ bC, with L the locked footprint, Aᵢ the incoming request's footprint and C the device capacity; b = 0.9 keeps a tenth free so reusable prefixes are not evicted the instant new work arrives. On 100k-turn traces, completion time falls 45.95% for Llama and 56.29% for GLM against HBM-only, and estimated write lifetime goes from 4.77 to 14.82 years on a chained 8+8 configuration, or 1.06 to 10.57 on a 4+4 shared-site one.

The authors are explicit about what this is: a request-level simulator with kernel latency models calibrated against H100 and B200 measurements, with no production HBF controller, no wear levelling, no full package-power model, and uniform wear assumed across the device. Lifetime in years is an arithmetic consequence of the assumed cycle budget, not a measurement — and SK hynix and Sandisk's own HBF disclosure in August gave capacity, bandwidth grades and the UCIe host interface but no endurance figure at all.

glossary.definition: NAND flash stacked and packaged like HBM and read over a wide die-to-die link; it trades far greater capacity per stack for much slower writes and a finite write budget.
One write-and-clear of a flash block. Each one damages the tunnel oxide slightly, so the rated count is a hard ceiling on total writes rather than a performance number.
The per-token keys and values a transformer keeps so it need not recompute attention over the whole prompt each step; it grows with context length, and it is what gets offloaded here.
Picojoules to move one bit across an interface — the figure that decides whether a memory tier is thermally affordable, independent of how fast it runs.

items.fab_angle: Endurance is a process number before it is a scheduling one: tunnel-oxide thickness, programming voltage and how many levels you ask a cell to resolve are what set the cycle count, and all three are traded against bits per cell. A serving policy written against a 100,000-cycle assumption is really a bet on a cell design nobody has published.

items.title: Directed Hamiltonicity drops below 2ⁿ for the first time since 1962
items.dek: Tomohiro Koana at the University of Tokyo and Soh Kumabe at CyberAgent give a randomised algorithm that decides whether a directed graph has a Hamiltonian cycle — a tour visiting every vertex exactly once — in about 1.9133ⁿ time, beating the 2ⁿ bound that has stood since 1962.
items.why_it_matters: The 2ⁿ bound was never an artefact of one algorithm; it is what falls out of the only idea anyone had, which is to remember, for each of the 2ⁿ subsets of vertices, which vertices a path covering that subset can end at. Every improvement since has either matched it or beaten it only on undirected or bipartite graphs, where edges can be paired up. Breaking it on general digraphs says the subset table is not the floor — and it gets there with algebra, counting solutions modulo two, rather than with a cleverer table. The margin is the honest part: 2ⁿ/1.9133ⁿ is only about 80 at n = 100.
items.background_md: Exact exponential algorithms are the part of complexity theory that cares what the exponent is. Nobody expects a polynomial algorithm for an NP-hard problem, so the live question becomes which constant sits in the base, and the gap between 2ⁿ and 1.9ⁿ compounds: it is the difference between a search that finishes and one that does not. Hamiltonian cycle — is there a tour visiting every vertex exactly once — is the canonical test case, and the Bellman–Held–Karp dynamic program of 1962 that solves it in 2ⁿ time is still the skeleton inside exact travelling-salesman solvers.
items.deeper_md:
The route is parity, not counting. The core subroutine computes the number of Hamiltonian paths modulo two at each total weight, in (2 − 2⁻ᵈ)ⁿ·poly(n,W) time, under the restriction that at most d distinct arc weights enter any single vertex. Keeping d small is what makes that bound good, and the paper buys it by randomly deleting and duplicating arcs and then partitioning the copies entering each vertex into d groups, so that choosing one group per vertex isolates a single Hamiltonian path — the isolation lemma applied to groups of arcs rather than to arcs.

With d = 3 the subroutine runs in (15/8)ⁿ = 1.875ⁿ, and the paper's own success probability (1 − 1/(1 + (2³ − 1)²))ⁿ⁻¹ = (49/50)ⁿ⁻¹ is the repetition factor you pay for it: 1.875 × 50/49 = 375/196 = 1.9133. Two pieces of machinery are borrowed — the generalised-Laplacian determinant method of Björklund, Kaski and Koutis (2017), and Arvind and Guruswami's random linearisation (2021).

The limits are stated. It is randomised, so a graph that has a Hamiltonian cycle can be missed. It is detection, not counting; exact counting remains at 2^(n−Ω(√n)). And 1.9133 is still a long way from the 1.657ⁿ Björklund reached on undirected graphs in 2010, which is the measure of how much harder direction makes this.

glossary.definition: Big-O with polynomial factors in n suppressed, used when the exponential base is the only quantity being compared and a factor of n³ is noise.
The 1962 dynamic program that tabulates, for every subset of vertices and every endpoint, whether a path covering that subset ends there; its table has 2ⁿ rows, which is where the 2ⁿ comes from.
Assign random weights and, with good probability, exactly one of the objects being counted has minimum weight; that turns "is the count nonzero" into "is the count odd", which algebra can answer.
Computing only a count's parity rather than the count. Over the two-element field a parity can be read off a determinant, which is why it is so much cheaper than the number itself.

items.title: RoPE's fast rotations buy position sense and cost semantic stability
items.dek: Yuyang Wu, Yufeng Du and Hao Peng show that rotary position embeddings — the rotations by which a transformer encodes how far apart two tokens sit — cannot both hold a token's preferences steady and separate adjacent positions past a context length the authors derive, and that rescaling only the fastest rotations recovers up to 25 accuracy points.
items.why_it_matters: Long-context failure has mostly been treated as one problem with one family of fixes: stretch the frequencies, or fine-tune on longer sequences. This splits it in two and makes each half measurable per attention head from activations already lying around. Reasoning tasks fail because a token's ranking against its competitors flips when the whole block is shifted along; retrieval tasks fail because adjacent positions stop being distinguishable at all. The two want opposite adjustments to the same rotation frequencies, which is a straightforward explanation for why a single global rescaling has been leaving accuracy unclaimed on both.
items.background_md: Attention has no built-in notion of order, so position has to be injected. Rotary embeddings do it by rotating each query and key vector within a set of two-dimensional planes, each plane turning at its own frequency, so that the dot product between a query at one position and a key at another depends only on the gap between them. Low-frequency planes barely turn across a long sequence and effectively carry content; high-frequency planes turn many times and carry fine positional detail. The frequency grid is fixed before training, and a model reading far past the lengths it saw meets rotation angles it never trained on.
items.deeper_md:
The theory's new ingredient is allowing query and key magnitudes to differ across frequencies, which trained models do and which earlier analyses assumed away. From that, Theorem 1 gives an M_max beyond which no fixed attention-score margin can satisfy both conditions: past it, either the probability of semantic reversal exceeds a tolerance δ or adjacent-position sensitivity falls below ζ. The bound depends on the frequency grid and the calibration error rather than on the weights, so it is a property of the encoding itself.

Both failures become scores computed from cached query and key activations at zero extra forward passes — a semantic score 1 − P_rev, where P_rev is the probability that shifting position reverses two keys' ranking, and a positional score, the mean normalised |S(m+1) − S(m)| over relative distances. Across 49 task settings drawn from nine benchmark sources, reasoning tasks score badly on the first and retrieval tasks on the second.

The fix is per-head and opposite in sign: attenuate or freeze high-frequency rotations in the heads most prone to reversal, amplify them by a scalar α > 1 in the rest. It needs no training and yields up to 20 percentage points on Qwen3-8B and 25 on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct — but it helps on only 63.3% and 65.3% of configurations, so a third see nothing, and the analysis is single-head and single-layer. The authors say plainly that the underlying tradeoff needs a different attention design, not a rescaling.

glossary.definition: Position encoded by rotating query and key vectors within fixed two-dimensional planes at a spread of frequencies, so an attention score depends on the distance between two tokens rather than their absolute indices.
One independent query/key/value projection inside a layer. Heads specialise, which is why a diagnosis that averages over them hides the very thing being diagnosed.
The set of rotation rates assigned to RoPE's planes, usually a geometric sequence; the fastest resolve nearby positions and the slowest barely move across the whole context.
The arithmetic difference between two accuracies rather than their ratio: 40% to 60% is 20 points and also a 50% relative gain, and conflating the two inflates results.

foundations.subtitle: Thirty-micrometre tin droplets, roughly a hundred thousand a second, converted into 13.5 nm light at about five percent — the least efficient step in the industry.
foundations.tldr: Nothing useful transmits at 13.5 nm and nothing convenient fluoresces there, so the only way to get extreme-ultraviolet light in quantity is to vaporise a tin droplet with a carbon-dioxide laser and collect what the resulting plasma radiates. About 5% of the laser energy comes back out as light the optics can actually reflect, and the theoretical ceiling is near 9%. Almost every constraint in advanced lithography — tool cost, wafer throughput, even resist chemistry — is downstream of that single percentage.

sections.heading: Why the light has to be made out of plasma
sections.body_md:
Start with the photon. Energy in electronvolts is 1239.8 divided by wavelength in nanometres, so a 13.5 nm photon carries 91.8 eV. That is far above the binding energy of the outer electrons in essentially every material, which means essentially every material absorbs it. There is no lens, no window, no fibre, and no gas you can propagate it through: an EUV tool is a vacuum chamber with mirrors in it, and the light is reflected rather than refracted from the moment it is born.

That also rules out the obvious ways of generating it. You cannot build a laser at 13.5 nm with a conventional gain medium, because the transitions at that energy belong to ions, not neutral atoms, and keeping a population of them inverted is not something anyone does at the kilowatt scale. What is left is thermal: make a plasma hot enough that its ions radiate near 13.5 nm, and collect the fraction of that emission going the right way. A production scanner wants more than 250 W of dose-controlled light inside the usable band — which sets the whole engineering problem.
sections.deeper_md: The constraint is sharper than "materials absorb." A multilayer reflector works by Bragg interference across a stack of many thin layer pairs, and interference of that kind is narrowband by construction — in this case the roughly 2% bandwidth around 13.5 nm that defines "in-band." That band was not chosen for the source's convenience; it is where a molybdenum/silicon stack happens to work. Everything about the tin plasma is therefore an attempt to put as much radiated power as possible inside a window the optics picked first.

sections.heading: Which tin ions actually do the work
sections.body_md:
Tin is not an arbitrary choice, and this is the part that explains why nobody has swapped it out. Strip eight to fourteen electrons off a tin atom and the remaining ion has a dense thicket of transitions between its 4p, 4d and 4f levels, all crowding into a narrow spectral region near 13.5 nm. Individually these lines are unresolvable; collectively they form what spectroscopists call an unresolved transition array, and it is bright precisely because so many different transitions pile into the same place.

To have Sn⁸⁺ through Sn¹⁴⁺ present in quantity you need the plasma's electron temperature in the 20 to 40 eV range. Hotter and the ionisation runs past the useful charge states; cooler and you never reach them. So the source is not being optimised for peak temperature — it is being held inside a window, and the width of that window is one reason the conversion efficiency cannot simply be dialled upward. The element and the optics were effectively co-selected: tin's array sits where molybdenum/silicon reflects.
sections.deeper_md: The same atomic structure that makes tin bright makes it opaque to its own light. The array that radiates at 13.5 nm also absorbs at 13.5 nm, so a plasma that is too dense or too thick reabsorbs photons before they escape — the physical reason conversion efficiency peaks and then falls as you push harder, rather than rising monotonically with laser energy.

sections.heading: Two pulses per droplet, and why the laser is a CO₂
sections.body_md:
A droplet generator throws liquid tin spheres about 30 µm across into the vacuum vessel at roughly 100 kHz. Each one is hit twice. A weak pre-pulse arrives first and does no useful radiating at all: its job is to deform the sphere into a thin, expanded sheet of tin vapour and small droplets, spreading the same mass over a much larger area. The main pulse then heats that pre-shaped target.

Why two? Because a laser couples into a plasma at its critical density — the density where the plasma frequency equals the laser frequency — and for a 10 µm carbon-dioxide laser that density is around 10¹⁹ cm⁻³. A compact liquid droplet presents a steep density gradient and most of the beam reflects or misses the right layer. The pre-pulse manufactures a target whose density profile matches where the main pulse can deposit energy. A 1 µm Nd:YAG laser couples at about 10²¹ cm⁻³ instead — a hundred times denser, and therefore far more self-absorbing, which is the main reason the industry settled on the longer wavelength.
sections.deeper_md: The wavelength choice is a chain of consequences, not a preference. Critical density scales as 1/λ², so a 10 µm driver deposits energy in a plasma two orders of magnitude thinner than a 1 µm driver would. Thinner plasma means less reabsorption of the 13.5 nm light on the way out, which is where the conversion-efficiency advantage comes from. The price is a laser that is physically enormous: the multi-stage master-oscillator power-amplifier chain and its beam path are a substantial fraction of the tool.

sections.heading: Conversion efficiency, and why it is the number that matters
sections.body_md:
Conversion efficiency is the fraction of drive-laser energy that leaves the plasma as in-band EUV. Industrial sources exceed 5.5%, against a theoretical limit near 9%. That is the number the whole tool is built around: at 5%, a 250 W in-band source needs a multi-kilowatt laser running continuously, and everything about the vessel, the cooling and the power draw follows.

It is also more fragile than a single figure suggests, because it depends on pulse shape as well as energy. One radiative-magnetohydrodynamic study of CO₂ pulses on liquid tin reports in-band conversion of 4% for a 30 ns pulse against 3.67% for a 240 ns pulse at the same energy, because the longer pulse lets the plasma expand while still being driven, and the expanded plasma reabsorbs more of its own emission. The same work finds a layer of relatively cold tin vapour at 1 to 2 g/cm³ forming between the liquid droplet and the low-density plasma — a sink for energy that never becomes light.
sections.deeper_md: Note the mismatch between the numbers quoted here, and treat it as information rather than noise. The ~5.5% figure comes from industrial systems with optimised pre-pulse shaping and dose control; the 4% and 3.67% figures come from a specific simulation of 150–180 µm droplets at 14 GW/cm² with pulse energies of 75–600 mJ and no pre-pulse. They are measuring different objects. Any single conversion-efficiency number you see quoted without its target preparation, pulse shape and collection geometry is close to meaningless.

sections.heading: Why the modelling is still argued about
sections.body_md:
A source like this cannot be designed by measurement alone — you cannot put a probe inside the plasma — so the numbers come from codes that couple radiation transport, hydrodynamics and atomic kinetics. In 2020 eight institutions from four countries ran the first EUV light sources code comparison workshop, benchmarking their codes against two deliberately simple problems: the atomic kinetics and radiative properties of tin plasma under EUV-generating conditions, and laser absorption in a fully ionised one-dimensional hydrogen plasma.

The interesting thing about that exercise is that it was necessary. A tin plasma at 30 eV contains ions in a dozen charge states, each with thousands of levels, and the opacity depends on which levels are populated, which depends on the radiation field, which depends on the opacity. Different codes make different truncations of that loop, and they do not land in the same place. When a vendor quotes a conversion efficiency from simulation, the honest reading is that it is a prediction from one set of truncations.
sections.deeper_md: The second benchmark — laser absorption in fully ionised hydrogen — looks trivially simple next to tin, and that is why it was chosen. If codes disagree on inverse bremsstrahlung absorption in a one-dimensional hydrogen plasma where the physics is analytic, the disagreement is numerical rather than physical, and you have found a problem you can actually fix. Benchmark design of that kind is how a modelling community establishes which of its disagreements are real.

sections.heading: The collector is the consumable
sections.body_md:
Here is the part the physics papers mention last and the fab notices first. Every droplet that radiates also sprays tin. Some of it lands on the collector — the multilayer mirror surrounding the plasma that gathers its emission and passes it into the scanner — and tin on a multilayer mirror absorbs exactly the light the mirror exists to reflect. Collector reflectivity therefore decays with operating hours, and collector lifetime is a direct term in tool availability.

In-vessel plasma etching is the standing mitigation, and the problem is that it loses the race: the rate is adequate for thin films and not for thick deposits or whole splashed droplets. One line of work goes after a phase transition instead. Cooling contaminated silicon-carbide and silicon surfaces with nitrogen vapour to between −30 and −50 °C converted adhesive tin deposits into loose grey tin within 24 hours, and stronger cooling to around −120 °C delaminated droplets outright.
sections.deeper_md: Grey tin is the α phase — a brittle semiconducting allotrope favoured at low temperature, which nucleates so slowly near room temperature that ordinary metallic tin persists indefinitely instead. The cryogenic route drives that nucleation deliberately, and the reason it cleans rather than merely transforms is that the two allotropes have different crystal structures and therefore different densities: the deposit cannot change phase and still fit the area it was bonded over, so it comes loose. Nothing dissolved it.

glossary.definition: The narrow spectral window around 13.5 nm that a molybdenum/silicon multilayer mirror actually reflects. EUV power outside it is waste heat, so every source figure is quoted in-band.
In-band EUV energy out divided by drive-laser energy in. Industrial tin sources exceed 5.5% with a theoretical limit near 9%, which is why the drive laser is measured in kilowatts.
A spectral feature made of so many overlapping ionic transitions that individual lines cannot be separated. Tin ions from Sn⁸⁺ to Sn¹⁴⁺ produce one near 13.5 nm, and it is the reason tin is the fuel.

The electron density at which the plasma frequency equals the laser frequency, so the laser can propagate no further and deposits its energy. It scales as 1/λ², which is why a 10 µm CO₂ driver couples near 10¹⁹ cm⁻³ and a 1 µm driver near 10²¹.

A weak pulse fired at the droplet before the main one. It radiates almost nothing; its purpose is to deform the droplet into an expanded low-density target whose density profile matches where the main pulse can couple.
The multilayer mirror surrounding the plasma that gathers its emission into the scanner. It is the first optic the tin reaches, so its contamination rate sets how often the source has to come down.
The brittle semiconducting allotrope of tin, favoured at low temperature but slow to nucleate; deliberately inducing it is one route to shedding tin deposits from a contaminated surface.

foundations.try_this: Do the photon arithmetic, then the mass arithmetic. First: photon energy in eV is 1239.8 divided by wavelength in nm, so 13.5 nm is 91.8 eV while a 405 nm near-UV source is 3.06 eV — thirty times less per photon. For the same dose in mJ/cm², work out how many photons land in one 20 nm × 20 nm area in each case; in ten minutes you will have derived the EUV shot-noise problem from scratch, and seen why a near-UV maskless stepper does not have it. Second: Versolato's review gives 30 µm tin droplets at roughly 100 kHz. Compute the volume of tin a source consumes in an eight-hour shift, look up tin's density to convert it to grams, and then read Böwering and Meier on what becomes of the fraction that lands on the collector.
